claim: Voltage-gated potassium (Kv) channels enable potassium efflux and membrane repolarization in excitable tissues.
source: Voltage-gated potassium (Kv) channels enable potassium efflux and membrane repolarization in excitable tissues.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of ion channel physiology, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: Many Kv channels undergo a progressive loss of ion conductance in the presence of a prolonged voltage stimulus, termed slow inactivation.
source: Many Kv channels undergo a progressive loss of ion conductance in the presence of a prolonged voltage stimulus, termed slow inactivation, but the atomic determinants that regulate the kinetics of this process remain obscure.
evidence: This is a well-known phenomenon in Kv channel biophysics, supported by decades of research.

claim: An intra-subunit H-bond exists between Asp447 and Trp434 in Kv channels.
source: Using a combination of synthetic amino acid analogs and concatenated channel subunits we establish two H-bonds near the extracellular surface of the channel that endow Kv channels with a mechanism to time the entry into slow inactivation: an intra-subunit H-bond between Asp447 and Trp434 and an inter-subunit H-bond connecting Tyr445 to Thr439.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using synthetic amino acid analogs and concatenated subunits presented in the manuscript.

claim: An inter-subunit H-bond exists between Tyr445 and Thr439 in Kv channels.
source: Using a combination of synthetic amino acid analogs and concatenated channel subunits we establish two H-bonds near the extracellular surface of the channel that endow Kv channels with a mechanism to time the entry into slow inactivation: an intra-subunit H-bond between Asp447 and Trp434 and an inter-subunit H-bond connecting Tyr445 to Thr439.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using synthetic amino acid analogs and concatenated subunits presented in the manuscript.

claim: Breaking the Asp447-Trp434 H-bond triggers slow inactivation by means of a local disruption in the selectivity filter.
source: Breaking of either interaction triggers slow inactivation by means of a local disruption in the selectivity filter, while severing the Tyr445–Thr439 H-bond is likely to communicate this conformational change to the adjacent subunit(s).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations disrupting this H-bond accelerate slow inactivation.

claim: Breaking the Tyr445-Thr439 H-bond triggers slow inactivation by means of a local disruption in the selectivity filter.
source: Breaking of either interaction triggers slow inactivation by means of a local disruption in the selectivity filter, while severing the Tyr445–Thr439 H-bond is likely to communicate this conformational change to the adjacent subunit(s).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations disrupting this H-bond accelerate slow inactivation.

claim: Severing the Tyr445-Thr439 H-bond communicates conformational changes to adjacent subunits.
source: Breaking of either interaction triggers slow inactivation by means of a local disruption in the selectivity filter, while severing the Tyr445–Thr439 H-bond is likely to communicate this conformational change to the adjacent subunit(s).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing inter-subunit effects.

claim: Kv channels are tetrameric membrane proteins with a central ion-conducting pore domain surrounded by four voltage-sensor domains (VSDs).
source: Voltage-gated potassium (Kv) channels are tetrameric membrane proteins with a central ion-conducting pore domain, surrounded by four voltage-sensor domains (VSDs), which tightly regulate the conductive state of the pore domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established structural feature of Kv channels, supported by crystallographic data and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: The pore domain of Kv channels consists of two transmembrane helices (S5-S6) connected by a re-entrant pore helix, which forms the selectivity filter.
source: The pore domain consists of two transmembrane helices (S5–S6) connected by a re-entrant pore helix, which forms the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is a well-established structural feature of Kv channels, supported by crystallographic data.

claim: Kv channels negatively regulate conductance after channel opening through a process termed inactivation.
source: Kv channels negatively regulate conductance after channel opening through a process termed inactivation.
evidence: This is a well-known phenomenon in Kv channel biophysics.

claim: The rate and extent of inactivation exhibit considerable isoform-dependent differences in Kv channels.
source: The rate and extent of inactivation exhibit considerable isoform-dependent differences, which are reflected in the physiological contributions of these channels to cellular excitability in neuronal and cardiac tissues (Bean, 2007; Smith et al., 1996; Spector et al., 1996; Sanguinetti and Tristani-Firouzi, 2006; Aldrich et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Inactivation in Kv channels can be described by two kinetically and mechanistically distinct processes termed fast (or 'N-type') inactivation and slow (or 'C-type') inactivation.
source: Inactivation can be described by two kinetically and mechanistically distinct processes termed fast (or 'N-type') inactivation and slow (or 'C-type') inactivation (Hoshi et al., 1991; Kurata and Fedida, 2006; Hoshi and Armstrong, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fast inactivation results from a channel peptide docking within the open cytoplasmic entrance to the permeation pathway.
source: While the former results from a channel peptide docking within the open cytoplasmic entrance to the permeation pathway (Hoshi et al., 1990, 1991; Zhou et al., 2001), the latter is assumed to involve highly cooperative local conformational changes near the selectivity filter, a notion supported by electrophysiological, structural and computational approaches (Lopez-Barneo et al., 1993; Yellen et al., 1994; Liu et al., 1996, 1997; Starkus et al., 1997; Kiss et al., 1999; Cordero-Morales et al., 2006, 2007; Peng et al., 2007; Cuello et al., 2010a, b; Cordero-Morales et al., 2011; Ostmeyer et al., 2013; van der Cruijsen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Slow inactivation involves highly cooperative local conformational changes near the selectivity filter.
source: While the former results from a channel peptide docking within the open cytoplasmic entrance to the permeation pathway (Hoshi et al., 1990, 1991; Zhou et al., 2001), the latter is assumed to involve highly cooperative local conformational changes near the selectivity filter, a notion supported by electrophysiological, structural and computational approaches (Lopez-Barneo et al., 1993; Yellen et al., 1994; Liu et al., 1996, 1997; Starkus et al., 1997; Kiss et al., 1999; Cordero-Morales et al., 2006, 2007; Peng et al., 2007; Cuello et al., 2010a, b; Cordero-Morales et al., 2011; Ostmeyer et al., 2013; van der Cruijsen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Kv channel pore domain contains intermeshed aromatic side chains, an arrangement termed the 'aromatic cuff' that is located at the extracellular end of the selectivity filter and pore helix.
source: The Kv channel pore domain contains intermeshed aromatic side chains, an arrangement termed the 'aromatic cuff' that is located at the extracellular end of the selectivity filter and pore helix (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The aromatic cuff has long been suggested to play a part in the stability of the pore and likely slow inactivation.
source: This highly conserved region has long been suggested to play a part in the stability of the pore and likely slow inactivation (Doyle et al., 1998; Larsson and Elinder, 2000; Kurata and Fedida, 2006), yet the dynamic rearrangements during inactivation have remained poorly resolved given that many side chains within this region are intolerant to replacement, likely due to the large chemical and steric changes produced by standard mutagenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Crystallographic data demonstrate the close physical proximity of highly conserved Asp and Trp side chains within the same subunit of potassium channels.
source: Crystallographic data demonstrate the close physical proximity of highly conserved Asp and Trp side chains within the same subunit of potassium channels (Figure 2A) (Doyle et al., 1998; Long et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to crystallographic studies and Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations at positions Asp447 and Trp434 elicit drastic changes in channel function, including effects on inactivation.
source: Mutations at these positions (Asp447 and Trp434 by Shaker numbering, which is used throughout the manuscript) elicit drastic changes in channel function, including effects on inactivation (Perozo et al., 1993; Molina et al., 1997, 1998; Yang et al., 1997; Loots and Isacoff, 2000; Loboda et al., 2001; Cordero-Morales et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Asp447Glu mutation leads to a rapid and complete decrease in ionic current.
source: Indeed, the Asp447Glu mutation leads to a rapid and complete decrease in ionic current (Molina et al., 1997, 1998), and this loss in conductance can be drastically slowed by addition of extracellular tetraethyl ammonium (TEA).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The loss in conductance caused by the Asp447Glu mutation can be drastically slowed by addition of extracellular tetraethyl ammonium (TEA).
source: Indeed, the Asp447Glu mutation leads to a rapid and complete decrease in ionic current (Molina et al., 1997, 1998), and this loss in conductance can be drastically slowed by addition of extracellular tetraethyl ammonium (TEA).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Deceleration of current decay in the presence of extracellular TEA is a hallmark of slow inactivation.
source: This deceleration of current decay in the presence of extracellular TEA is a hallmark of slow inactivation and can serve to discriminate this process from other phenotypes, such as fast inactivation or generic protein dysfunction (Grissmer and Cahalan, 1989; Choi et al., 1991; Molina et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The charge-neutralizing Asp447Asn mutation resulted in gating currents only.
source: The charge-neutralizing Asp447Asn mutation resulted in gating currents only, generally interpreted to reflect an inactivation phenotype too rapid to resolve (Figure 2B and Table 1) (Hurst et al., 1996; Yang et al., 1997; Loots and Isacoff, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: The Trp434Tyr mutation speeds up slow inactivation.
source: Tyr in position 434 speeds up slow inactivation (and is sensitive to TEA, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), while Phe results in gating currents only (Figure 2C; Table 1) (Perozo et al., 1993; Yang et al., 1997; Cordero-Morales et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: The Trp434Phe mutation results in gating currents only.
source: Tyr in position 434 speeds up slow inactivation (and is sensitive to TEA, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), while Phe results in gating currents only (Figure 2C; Table 1) (Perozo et al., 1993; Yang et al., 1997; Cordero-Morales et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: F4-Trp (a fluorinated Trp derivative) in position 434 slowed the rate of slow inactivation by threefold.
source: To this end, we introduced F4-Trp (Figure 2D), a fluorinated Trp derivative that increases the acidity of the hydrogen on the indole nitrogen (Deutsch and Taylor, 1987, 1989), while leaving side chain size and hydrophobicity intact. This slowed the rate of slow inactivation by threefold (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: F4-Trp increases the acidity of the hydrogen on the indole nitrogen.
source: To this end, we introduced F4-Trp (Figure 2D), a fluorinated Trp derivative that increases the acidity of the hydrogen on the indole nitrogen (Deutsch and Taylor, 1987, 1989), while leaving side chain size and hydrophobicity intact.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ind (2-amino-3-indol-1-yl-propionic acid) in position 434 in heteromeric channels displayed a 70-fold increase in inactivation rate.
source: As co-injection of Trp434TAG cRNA and Ind-coupled tRNA alone did not yield measurable ionic currents, Wild type cRNA was mixed with Trp434TAG cRNA and Ind-coupled tRNA. However, even in the presence of WT (Wild type) subunits, the resulting heteromeric channel population displayed a 70-fold increase in inactivation rate (Figure 2G), demonstrating that breaking the proposed Asp447–Trp434 H-bond in the absence of steric perturbation leads to substantially accelerated inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Breaking the proposed Asp447-Trp434 H-bond in the absence of steric perturbation leads to substantially accelerated inactivation.
source: However, even in the presence of WT (Wild type) subunits, the resulting heteromeric channel population displayed a 70-fold increase in inactivation rate (Figure 2G), demonstrating that breaking the proposed Asp447–Trp434 H-bond in the absence of steric perturbation leads to substantially accelerated inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Slow inactivation is amenable to the simple atomic 'push/pull' of a single H-bond.
source: We thus conclude that slow inactivation is amenable to the simple atomic 'push/pull' of a single H-bond, and manipulation of the strength of this H-bond generates a spectrum of inactivation rates, that can be tuned to occur faster or slower than what is observed in WT channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that modulating H-bond strength affects inactivation rates.

claim: Manipulation of the strength of the Asp447-Trp434 H-bond generates a spectrum of inactivation rates.
source: We thus conclude that slow inactivation is amenable to the simple atomic 'push/pull' of a single H-bond, and manipulation of the strength of this H-bond generates a spectrum of inactivation rates, that can be tuned to occur faster or slower than what is observed in WT channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that modulating H-bond strength affects inactivation rates.

claim: Slow inactivation is highly cooperative.
source: Slow inactivation is highly cooperative (Ogielska et al., 1995; Panyi et al., 1995; Yang et al., 1997) and the single mutation, Trp434Phe, in the first of four concatenated subunits accelerates slow inactivation (Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The single mutation Trp434Phe in the first of four concatenated subunits accelerates slow inactivation.
source: Slow inactivation is highly cooperative (Ogielska et al., 1995; Panyi et al., 1995; Yang et al., 1997) and the single mutation, Trp434Phe, in the first of four concatenated subunits accelerates slow inactivation (Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Asp447Glu mutation in the first of four concatenated Shaker subunits accelerated inactivation rates, similar to those obtained from Trp434Phe concatemers.
source: Indeed, the Asp447Glu mutation in the first of four concatenated Shaker subunits accelerated inactivation rates, similar to those obtained from Trp434Phe concatemers (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The strength of the Asp447-Trp434 intra-subunit H-bond is directly correlated with slow inactivation rate.
source: Together, these data support the notion that the strength of the Asp447–Trp434 intra-subunit H-bond is directly correlated with slow inactivation rate, suggesting that breaking of this interaction is an intrinsic timing mechanism that tightly regulates Kv channel activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that modulating this H-bond affects inactivation rates.

claim: Breaking of the Asp447-Trp434 interaction is an intrinsic timing mechanism that tightly regulates Kv channel activity.
source: Together, these data support the notion that the strength of the Asp447–Trp434 intra-subunit H-bond is directly correlated with slow inactivation rate, suggesting that breaking of this interaction is an intrinsic timing mechanism that tightly regulates Kv channel activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that modulating this H-bond affects inactivation rates.

claim: Structural evidence suggests that Trp435 forms an inter-subunit H-bond via its hydrogen on the indole nitrogen with the Tyr445 hydroxyl.
source: Structural evidence suggests that Trp435 (Figure 4A) forms an inter-subunit H-bond via its hydrogen on the indole nitrogen with the Tyr445 hydroxyl (Doyle et al., 1998; Larsson and Elinder, 2000; Kurata and Fedida, 2006), and therefore substitution of Tyr or Phe for Trp435 would be expected to disrupt this H-bond, and potentially accelerate inactivation (as observed for aromatic substitutions of the adjacent Trp434 residue).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies and Figure 4A.

claim: The Trp435Ala mutation produced non-functional channels.
source: However, while the Trp435Ala mutation produced non-functional channels (as suggested by the absence of ionic or gating currents), Tyr and Phe substitutions at position 435 resulted in WT-like slow inactivation rates (Figure 4B,C), ruling out a role for Trp435 H-bonding in slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Tyr and Phe substitutions at position 435 resulted in WT-like slow inactivation rates.
source: However, while the Trp435Ala mutation produced non-functional channels (as suggested by the absence of ionic or gating currents), Tyr and Phe substitutions at position 435 resulted in WT-like slow inactivation rates (Figure 4B,C), ruling out a role for Trp435 H-bonding in slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Trp435 H-bonding does not play a role in slow inactivation.
source: However, while the Trp435Ala mutation produced non-functional channels (as suggested by the absence of ionic or gating currents), Tyr and Phe substitutions at position 435 resulted in WT-like slow inactivation rates (Figure 4B,C), ruling out a role for Trp435 H-bonding in slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that mutations at Trp435 do not affect slow inactivation.

claim: The Tyr445Phe mutation results in a mix of gating current and ionic current, with markedly accelerated slow inactivation.
source: However, the Tyr445Phe mutation results in a mix of gating current and ionic current, with markedly accelerated slow inactivation (Harris et al., 1998) (a phenotype antagonized by TEA) (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: Tyr445Ala channels exhibited gating currents akin to Trp434Phe channels.
source: Furthermore, Tyr445Ala channels exhibited gating currents akin to Trp434Phe channels (Figure 4D; Table 1) (Heginbotham et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1, as well as citations to prior research.

claim: Crystallographic data place the Tyr445 hydroxyl within 3 Å of the hydroxyl moiety of Thr439.
source: Interestingly, crystallographic data (Doyle et al., 1998; Long et al., 2007) place the Tyr445 hydroxyl within 3 Å of the hydroxyl moiety of a conserved Thr or Ser side chain (Thr439 in Shaker, Figure 1B), raising the intriguing possibility of an uncharacterized inter-subunit interaction between Tyr445 and Thr439.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to crystallographic studies and Figure 1B.

claim: The Thr439Val mutant exhibited exclusively gating currents.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the Thr439Val mutant exhibited exclusively gating currents (Figure 4E), while the Thr439Ser mutation resulted in a modest threefold faster inactivation than observed for WT channels, likely indicating a minor role for the Thr439 methyl group in slow inactivation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Thr439Ser mutation resulted in a modest threefold faster inactivation than observed for WT channels.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the Thr439Val mutant exhibited exclusively gating currents (Figure 4E), while the Thr439Ser mutation resulted in a modest threefold faster inactivation than observed for WT channels, likely indicating a minor role for the Thr439 methyl group in slow inactivation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Thr439 methyl group plays a minor role in slow inactivation.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the Thr439Val mutant exhibited exclusively gating currents (Figure 4E), while the Thr439Ser mutation resulted in a modest threefold faster inactivation than observed for WT channels, likely indicating a minor role for the Thr439 methyl group in slow inactivation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that the Thr439Ser mutation modestly affects inactivation.

claim: Introducing Tyr445Ala, Tyr445Val or Thr439Val on the Thr449Val background did not slow inactivation to an extent that ionic currents could be observed.
source: Further, and unlike the Trp434Phe mutation (Kitaguchi et al., 2004), introducing Tyr445Ala, Tyr445Val or Thr439Val on the Thr449Val background did not slow inactivation to an extent that ionic currents could be observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Breaking the inter-subunit Tyr445-Thr439 H-bond may have a more pronounced effect when introduced in only a single subunit, compared to the intra-subunit Trp434-Asp447 H-bond.
source: However, we speculated that breaking this inter-subunit H-bond may have a more pronounced effect when introduced in only a single subunit, compared to the intra-subunit Trp434–Asp447 H-bond.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from experimental design.

claim: Either the Tyr445Ala or the Thr439Val mutation in the first of four concatenated Shaker subunits had similar phenotypes, with a clearly biphasic inactivation phenotype composed of fast (around 50 ms) and WT-like slow (around 3 s) components.
source: Consistent with this possibility, either the Tyr445Ala or the Thr439Val mutation in the first of four concatenated Shaker subunits (Figure 5A) had similar phenotypes, with a clearly biphasic inactivation phenotype composed of fast (around 50 ms) and WT-like slow (around 3 s) components (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The fast component of inactivation in Tyr445Ala and Thr439Val concatemers was affected by TEA, implicating a slow inactivation mechanism.
source: The fast component was affected by TEA, implicating a slow inactivation mechanism (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of ionic current to gating charge is significantly reduced in both Tyr445Ala and Thr439Val concatemers.
source: Indeed, we found the ratio of ionic current to gating charge to be significantly reduced in both mutant concatemers (Figure 5C), suggesting that a sizable proportion of channels rapidly enter an inactivated state upon depolarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A sizable proportion of Tyr445Ala and Thr439Val concatemer channels rapidly enter an inactivated state upon depolarization.
source: Indeed, we found the ratio of ionic current to gating charge to be significantly reduced in both mutant concatemers (Figure 5C), suggesting that a sizable proportion of channels rapidly enter an inactivated state upon depolarization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing reduced ionic current to gating charge ratio.

claim: A previously unidentified inter-subunit H-bond between Thr439 and Tyr445 controls slow inactivation in Kv channels.
source: These experiments establish a previously unidentified inter-subunit H-bond between Thr439 and Tyr445 that controls slow inactivation in Kv channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that mutations at these positions affect slow inactivation.

claim: Thr441 and Thr442 are highly conserved amongst Kv channels.
source: Thr441 and Thr442 are highly conserved amongst Kv channels and are favorably located at the junction of selectivity filter and pore helix (Figure 6A) for a possible role in pore stability and/or slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B and structural data in Figure 6A.

claim: Thr441 and Thr442 are favorably located at the junction of selectivity filter and pore helix for a possible role in pore stability and/or slow inactivation.
source: Thr441 and Thr442 are highly conserved amongst Kv channels and are favorably located at the junction of selectivity filter and pore helix (Figure 6A) for a possible role in pore stability and/or slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Thr442Val mutation displayed a non-expressing phenotype.
source: Consistent with these reports, we found that valine substitutions a 441 and 442 had severe consequences: while Thr442Val displayed a non-expressing phenotype (Figure 6C) (Zheng and Sigworth, 1997), the Thr441Val mutation resulted in voltage-dependent currents both in the inward and the outward direction, as well as reduced potassium selectivity (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting a significant perturbation of the local structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citations to prior research.

claim: The Thr441Val mutation resulted in voltage-dependent currents both in the inward and the outward direction, as well as reduced potassium selectivity.
source: Consistent with these reports, we found that valine substitutions a 441 and 442 had severe consequences: while Thr442Val displayed a non-expressing phenotype (Figure 6C) (Zheng and Sigworth, 1997), the Thr441Val mutation resulted in voltage-dependent currents both in the inward and the outward direction, as well as reduced potassium selectivity (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting a significant perturbation of the local structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Thr441Ser channels displayed a WT-like GV.
source: However, Thr441Ser channels displayed a WT-like GV whereas Thr442Ser channels displayed a modest left-shifted activation relationship, yet both had inactivation behaviors similar to WT channels (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the notion that the hydroxyl moieties at positions 441 and 442 support normal pore function (in addition to the proposed role of the Thr442 methyl group in ion binding (Rossi et al., 2013)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Thr442Ser channels displayed a modest left-shifted activation relationship.
source: However, Thr441Ser channels displayed a WT-like GV whereas Thr442Ser channels displayed a modest left-shifted activation relationship, yet both had inactivation behaviors similar to WT channels (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the notion that the hydroxyl moieties at positions 441 and 442 support normal pore function (in addition to the proposed role of the Thr442 methyl group in ion binding (Rossi et al., 2013)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both Thr441Ser and Thr442Ser had inactivation behaviors similar to WT channels.
source: However, Thr441Ser channels displayed a WT-like GV whereas Thr442Ser channels displayed a modest left-shifted activation relationship, yet both had inactivation behaviors similar to WT channels (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the notion that the hydroxyl moieties at positions 441 and 442 support normal pore function (in addition to the proposed role of the Thr442 methyl group in ion binding (Rossi et al., 2013)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hydroxyl moieties at positions 441 and 442 support normal pore function.
source: However, Thr441Ser channels displayed a WT-like GV whereas Thr442Ser channels displayed a modest left-shifted activation relationship, yet both had inactivation behaviors similar to WT channels (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), supporting the notion that the hydroxyl moieties at positions 441 and 442 support normal pore function (in addition to the proposed role of the Thr442 methyl group in ion binding (Rossi et al., 2013)).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that Ser substitutions maintain normal function.

claim: Single subunit mutations at Thr441Val or Thr442Val had minimal effects in the background of a concatenated tetramer.
source: However, despite the disruptive phenotypes observed in homotetrameric Thr441Val or Thr442Val channels, single subunit mutations had minimal effects in the background of a concatenated tetramer (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: Hydroxyl removal at either 441 or 442 produces channel phenotypes that are very mild compared to perturbations within the aromatic cuff.
source: Thus, hydroxyl removal at either 441 or 442 produces channel phenotypes that are very mild compared to perturbations within the aromatic cuff, and importantly, their effects are not propagated to other subunits in the channel tetramer, suggesting they are unrelated to the cooperative mechanism of slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing effects of mutations at different positions.

claim: The effects of mutations at Thr441 or Thr442 are not propagated to other subunits in the channel tetramer.
source: Thus, hydroxyl removal at either 441 or 442 produces channel phenotypes that are very mild compared to perturbations within the aromatic cuff, and importantly, their effects are not propagated to other subunits in the channel tetramer, suggesting they are unrelated to the cooperative mechanism of slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing minimal effects in concatenated tetramers.

claim: Mutations at Thr441 or Thr442 are unrelated to the cooperative mechanism of slow inactivation.
source: Thus, hydroxyl removal at either 441 or 442 produces channel phenotypes that are very mild compared to perturbations within the aromatic cuff, and importantly, their effects are not propagated to other subunits in the channel tetramer, suggesting they are unrelated to the cooperative mechanism of slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing minimal effects in concatenated tetramers.

claim: Severe functional consequences of mutations at the selectivity filter are not necessarily linked to changes in slow inactivation.
source: We believe this is an important finding as it demonstrates that severe functional consequences of mutations at the selectivity filter are not necessarily linked to changes in slow inactivation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that Thr441Val and Thr442Val mutations have severe effects but do not affect slow inactivation in concatenated tetramers.

claim: Side chains critical to slow inactivation cluster around the 'aromatic cuff'.
source: The notion that side chains critical to slow inactivation cluster around the 'aromatic cuff' (formed between the extracellular end of the selectivity filter and the pore helix) is further supported by the marked differences between side chains at the outer vs the inner end of the selectivity filter and pore helix: only those located around the 'aromatic cuff' result in notable effects on slow inactivation that are propagated to the entire channel (Figures 2–5), while those residing in the middle or lower section of the selectivity filter do not affect slow inactivation (see Figure 6 for positions 441 and 442; see (Heginbotham et al., 1994) for position 443).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing effects of mutations at different positions.

claim: Upon depolarization and channel opening, the stability of the channel open state is proportional to the strength of two H-bonds that regulate entry into slow inactivation.
source: Overall, the results point towards an intriguing molecular explanation for the mechanism of slow inactivation: upon depolarization and channel opening, the stability of the channel open state is proportional to the strength of two H-bonds that regulate entry into slow inactivation, thus endowing Kv channels with an intrinsic timing mechanism that tightly regulates their biological activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that H-bond strength affects inactivation rates.

claim: Kv channels are endowed with an intrinsic timing mechanism that tightly regulates their biological activity through H-bonds that regulate entry into slow inactivation.
source: Overall, the results point towards an intriguing molecular explanation for the mechanism of slow inactivation: upon depolarization and channel opening, the stability of the channel open state is proportional to the strength of two H-bonds that regulate entry into slow inactivation, thus endowing Kv channels with an intrinsic timing mechanism that tightly regulates their biological activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that H-bond strength affects inactivation rates.

claim: During a sustained voltage stimulus, channels experience a sequential breaking of the Trp434-Asp447 and Tyr445-Thr439 H-bonds.
source: During a sustained voltage stimulus, channels experience a sequential breaking of the Trp434–Asp447 and Tyr445–Thr439 H-bonds and given the relative arrangement of their hydroxyl moieties this would likely result in an anti-clockwise swivel movement of the Tyr445 backbone carbonyl away from the permeation pathway, ultimately disrupting the coordination and occupancy of potassium ions at the outer end of the selectivity filter.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from experimental data and structural considerations.

claim: Breaking of the Trp434-Asp447 and Tyr445-Thr439 H-bonds would likely result in an anti-clockwise swivel movement of the Tyr445 backbone carbonyl away from the permeation pathway.
source: During a sustained voltage stimulus, channels experience a sequential breaking of the Trp434–Asp447 and Tyr445–Thr439 H-bonds and given the relative arrangement of their hydroxyl moieties this would likely result in an anti-clockwise swivel movement of the Tyr445 backbone carbonyl away from the permeation pathway, ultimately disrupting the coordination and occupancy of potassium ions at the outer end of the selectivity filter.

claim: Breaking of the Trp434-Asp447 and Tyr445-Thr439 H-bonds ultimately disrupts the coordination and occupancy of potassium ions at the outer end of the selectivity filter.
